description: Command reference: cheat sheets for Git, PowerShell, Bash and Linux administration, and the network and security platforms most often met in the field. Commands are grouped by task so the same question can be answered on any platform, and the search looks across all of them at once.

vendors.name: Git
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. The commands of a working day with Git, from the first commit to recovering one that seemed lost. Placeholders are written in angle brackets or as example names.

commands.description: The name written in every commit made on this machine.
The address written in every commit; use the one your Git host knows, so commits link to your account.
New repositories start on a branch named main.
Every setting in effect, and the file each one comes from.
Makes the current folder a repository.
Copies a repository with its whole history into a new folder.
The branch, the staged and unstaged changes, and the untracked files.
The changes not staged yet.
The changes staged for the next commit.
The history of every branch as a compact graph.
Every change made to one file, with the differences.
One commit: its message, author and changes.
Who last changed each line, and in which commit.
Stages a file for the next commit.
Stages chosen parts of the changes, piece by piece.
Records the staged changes.
Rewrites the last commit with what is staged, or with a new message. Only before it is pushed.
Throws away the unstaged changes of a file. This cannot be undone.
Unstages a file and keeps its changes.
Creates a branch and moves to it.
Moves to an existing branch.
The local branches and the remote ones.
Joins a branch into the current one.
Replays the current branch on top of main, for a straight history. Not on a branch other people work on.
Deletes a merged branch; -D deletes it even if it is not merged.
The remotes and their addresses.
Downloads the new commits and forgets the remote branches deleted, without touching your files.
Fetches, then replays your local commits on top of what arrived.
Publishes a branch and remembers where it goes, so the next git push needs no argument.
Replaces the remote branch after a rebase, but refuses if someone pushed in the meantime.
A new commit that undoes an old one: the safe way on a shared branch.
Undoes the last commit and keeps its changes staged.
Makes the branch match the remote, discarding local commits and changes.
Everywhere HEAD has been: finds a commit that seemed lost after a reset or a rebase.
Puts uncommitted changes aside; git stash pop brings them back.
Copies one commit onto the current branch.
Finds the commit that brought a bug by halving the history; mark each step with git bisect good or git bisect bad.
An annotated tag on the current commit; publish it with git push origin v1.2.0.
Lists the untracked files and folders that git clean -fd would delete.
Stops tracking a file that should have been ignored, and keeps it on disk. Add it to .gitignore as well.

vendors.name: PowerShell
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. The verbs that say what a command does, what can follow a |, the operators, objects and classes, error handling, and the commands a Windows administrator reaches for every day. Most of it works in Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7; what is 7 only says so.

commands.description: Reads and never changes anything: Get-Service, Get-Process, Get-ChildItem.
Changes something that exists: Set-Service, Set-Content, Set-ItemProperty.
Creates or deletes: New-Item, New-LocalUser, Remove-Item.
Adds to a container, or empties it: Add-LocalGroupMember, Clear-DnsClientCache.
Runs or ends something that keeps running: Start-Service, Stop-Process, Restart-Computer.
Turns on or off: Enable-NetAdapter, Disable-LocalUser.
Answers true or false, or with a result to judge: Test-Path, Test-NetConnection.
Runs something: Invoke-Command, Invoke-WebRequest, Invoke-RestMethod.
Writes to a file or reads from one: Export-Csv, Import-Csv, Export-Clixml.
Changes format in memory, without a file: ConvertTo-Json, ConvertFrom-Json, ConvertTo-Html.
The approved verbs, and what each is for: use them in your own functions.
Every command whose name holds dns.
The commands of a module.
Worked examples of a command; -Online opens its page.
The about_ topics explain the language itself: about_Pipelines, about_Classes, about_Try_Catch_Finally.
The type of the objects a command returns, and their properties and methods.
What an alias stands for: ls, dir and gci are all Get-ChildItem.
The version of PowerShell and of its runtime.
Keeps the objects that match. The braced form takes any condition: Where-Object { $_.CPU -gt 100 }.
Sorts by a property and keeps the first ones.

commands.command: Get-Process | Select-Object Name, Id, @{ Name = 'MemoryMB'; Expression = { [math]::Round($_.WorkingSet64 / 1MB) } }
commands.description: Chooses properties, and computes new ones with a name and an expression.
Groups objects by a property, with a count per group.
Count, sum, average, minimum and maximum of a property.
Runs a block for each object, $_ being the current one. PowerShell 7 adds -Parallel.
Writes objects to a CSV file; Import-Csv reads them back as objects.
Objects as JSON; ConvertFrom-Json turns JSON back into objects.
A filterable window; the rows selected carry on down the pipeline.
Keeps a copy in a variable or a file while the pipeline goes on.
Formats for reading only. Put Format-* last: nothing can use what it outputs.
Comparisons. Text compares without regard to case; -ceq and the other c forms respect it.
Wildcard match with * and ?; -notlike is the opposite.
Regular expression match; the groups found are in $Matches. The Regex tool in Tools tests a pattern.
Whether a list holds a value.
Splits text into a list, or joins a list into text.
Replaces by regular expression; $1 in the replacement is the first group, in single quotes.
Formats values into text.
Boolean logic. -and and -or have the same precedence: group with parentheses.
Null coalescing and null conditional access, PowerShell 7 only.
Keeps the objects themselves, with their properties, not their text.
Converts a value to a type.
An array. += builds a new copy each time: use a [System.Collections.Generic.List[object]] for thousands of items.
A hashtable of keys and values; [ordered] @{} keeps them in order.
An object with properties: the way a script returns a result.
A class, with typed properties, a default value and a method using $this.
Creates an instance of a class. Static members use ::, as in [math]::Round(2.567, 1).
Environment variables.
The parameters of a script or a function, with a required one and a default value.
An advanced function, which gains -Verbose, -ErrorAction and the other common parameters.
Catches an error. -ErrorAction Stop turns an ordinary error into one catch receives.
The exit code of the last program run outside PowerShell, such as ping or robocopy.
Fails on an undefined variable or property instead of reading it as nothing.
Allows scripts for this session only, and changes nothing on the machine.
Records everything typed and printed until Stop-Transcript.
Runs a block on another machine over WinRM; Enter-PSSession srv01 opens an interactive session.

commands.command: Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption, Version, LastBootUpTime
commands.description: The edition, the build and the last start.
Restarts a service, and those that depend on it.
Ends processes by name.
The errors of the System log in the last day, filtered by the event log itself rather than afterwards.
Whether a TCP port answers, with the address and interface used.
A DNS query for any record type.
The address, gateway and DNS servers of each adapter.
The log files not written for 30 days.
The end of a log, followed as lines are written.
The lines matching a pattern across files, with the file and line number.
Who is a local administrator.
The last updates installed.
The owner and the permissions of a file or folder.

vendors.name: Bash
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. Writing Bash on a server or in a script: quoting, expansions, conditions and loops, functions and exit codes, redirections, arrays. Quote your variables: "$name" rather than $name, or a space in a value splits it into two arguments.

commands.description: Sets a variable. No space around the =.
Double quotes expand variables; single quotes keep the text exactly as written.
Braces separate the name from the text that follows.
Command substitution: what a command prints, in a variable.
Makes a variable visible to the programs the shell starts.
A variable that cannot be changed afterwards.
Removes the shortest matching end: report.log becomes report.
Removes the longest matching start: the file name of a path, as basename gives.
The value, or default when the variable is unset or empty.
Stops the script with the message when the variable is unset or empty.
The length of the value.
Replaces every occurrence in the value.
Tests a file: -d a folder, -e anything, -z an empty string, -n a non empty one.
Compares numbers with -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge; == and != compare text.
Matches a regular expression, unquoted; the groups are in BASH_REMATCH.

commands.command: for host in web01 web02 db01; do ping -c1 "$host"; done
commands.description: Loops over a list.

commands.command: while IFS= read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < hosts.txt
commands.description: Reads a file line by line, keeping spaces and backslashes.

commands.command: case "$1" in start) echo starting ;; stop) echo stopping ;; *) echo "usage: $0 start|stop" ;; esac
commands.description: Chooses by pattern.
Runs the second command only if the first succeeds, the third if either fails.
A function; local keeps a variable inside it, $1 is its first argument.
All the arguments as separate words, their number, and the script name.
The exit code of the last command: 0 is success, anything else a failure.
Stops at the first failing command, on an unset variable, and on a failure anywhere in a pipeline.
Cleans up when the script ends, even after an error.
Ends the script with an exit code the caller can test.
Output and errors into one file; >> appends instead of replacing.
Throws away the errors.
Shows the output and appends it to a file at the same time.
A here document, ended by a line holding only EOF. With the quotes, $ and backticks inside are kept as written.
Process substitution: the output of a command used where a file is expected.
Runs a command for each line of input, four at a time.
An array and all its items.
The number of items, and the first one.
An associative array, Bash 4 and later.

commands.command: shopt -s nullglob globstar; for f in **/*.log; do echo "$f"; done
commands.description: ** goes through folders recursively, and a pattern matching nothing expands to nothing.

vendors.name: Linux system administration
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. Files, permissions, processes and services, packages, disks and remote access on a Linux server: the networking and firewalling commands have platforms of their own below.

commands.description: Every file, hidden ones included, with permissions, owner and a readable size.
Files matching a name and unchanged for 30 days; add -delete to remove them.
The size of each folder, the largest last.
The free space of each mounted file system.
Follows a log as lines are written.
Searches text through folders, without regard to case, with line numbers.
A compressed archive; tar xzf backup.tgz -C /restore extracts it.
Copies only what changed, and mirrors deletions. The trailing slash of the source means its content.
Sets permissions in octal or symbolic form. The chmod tool in Tools builds both.
Changes the owner and the group, recursively.
A root shell, or one command as another user.
The identifiers of a user and the groups it belongs to.
Creates a user with a home folder, then sets its password.
Adds a user to a group. Without -a, the user leaves every group not listed.
Sets or reads an access control list, for permissions beyond owner, group and others.
The processes using the most memory.
Live processor and memory use per process; htop is friendlier where installed.
Asks a process to stop, or forces it when it does not.
The state of a service, its main process and its last log lines.

commands.command: systemctl restart nginx / systemctl enable --now nginx
commands.description: Restarts a service, or starts it now and at every boot.
The units that failed.
The log of one service since a time; -f follows it, -b shows it since the last boot.
Refreshes the package lists and upgrades, on Debian and Ubuntu.

commands.command: apt install nginx / apt remove nginx
commands.description: Installs or removes a package on Debian and Ubuntu.
The same on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Rocky, AlmaLinux and Fedora.

commands.command: dpkg -l | grep nginx / rpm -qa | grep nginx
commands.description: Whether a package is installed, and which version.
The distribution and its version, and the kernel version.
How long since the start, the load, and who is signed in.
Memory and swap, used and free.
Disks and partitions, with their file systems and mount points.
Mounts a partition; /etc/fstab lists what is mounted at boot.
The latest kernel messages with readable times: disks, USB devices, drivers.
The clock, the time zone and the NTP state; the host name.
Signs in with a key. The SSH keys tool in Tools generates one.
Adds your public key to the server, so the next sign-in needs no password.
Copies a file over SSH; rsync over SSH is quicker for folders.
Forwards a local port to a host the server can reach: open https://localhost:8443.
Edits or lists your scheduled jobs. The Crontab tool in Tools writes and explains the schedule.
The last sign-ins, with where they came from.

vendors.name: Active Directory
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. Users, groups and computers with the ActiveDirectory PowerShell module (RSAT, or a domain controller), then the domain controller, replication and Group Policy commands. Examples use the contoso.com domain.

commands.description: Every attribute of a user, LastLogonDate, pwdLastSet, lockoutTime and memberOf included.
Enabled accounts unused for 90 days. LastLogonDate replicates with up to 14 days of delay, which is fine at that scale.
Locked-out accounts; pipe to Unlock-ADAccount to unlock them.
Unlocks an account. If it locks again, something is retrying an old password: the security event triage names the source.
Resets a password and makes the user choose a new one at next sign-in.
The groups a user is a direct member of.
Every member of a group, through nested groups.
Adds a member. It counts from the user's next sign-in, or once their tickets are renewed.
Creates an enabled user in an OU.
Minimum length, history, maximum age and lockout settings of the domain password policy.
Password policies that override the domain one for specific groups.

commands.command: Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties OperatingSystem, OperatingSystemVersion, LastLogonDate | Sort-Object LastLogonDate
commands.description: Every computer with its Windows version and its last contact with the domain.
Whether this computer's trust with the domain works. Windows PowerShell 5.1.
Repairs a broken trust with a domain account, without leaving and joining the domain again. Restart afterwards.
Moves a computer to another OU, and so under other GPOs.
Computers silent for 90 days, ready to disable: remove -WhatIf once the list is checked.
The domain controller this machine finds, its site and what it offers (GC, KDC, time).
Every domain controller of the domain.
The domain controllers holding the five FSMO roles.
Replication health of every domain controller: largest delta, failures and their error.
The replication partners of one domain controller and the last result for each partition.
Forces replication of every partition, across sites, pushing from this domain controller.
Runs the domain controller tests and prints only what fails.
The DNS tests of a domain controller: registration, forwarders and delegation.
The SRV records clients use to find a domain controller.
The time offset of every domain controller; the PDC emulator should follow a reliable source.
The GPOs applied and filtered out, for this computer and the signed-in user.
The full report, with the winning GPO for every setting.
Applies computer and user policies again, now.

commands.command: Get-GPO -All | Sort-Object ModificationTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 DisplayName, ModificationTime
commands.description: The ten GPOs changed last: the first place to look after 'it worked yesterday'.
Every setting of one GPO, as a report.
Backs up every GPO before a change; Restore-GPO puts one back.
Deleted objects still in the Active Directory recycle bin.
Restores a deleted user with its attributes and group memberships, when the recycle bin is enabled.
Users inactive for 12 weeks, where the PowerShell module is not installed.

vendors.name: Windows command line (CMD)
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. The classic Windows commands that work in any prompt, recovery environment included: copies and permissions, services and tasks, disks and start-up, logs and certificates. Run them from an elevated prompt when they change the system.

commands.description: Mirrors a folder: copies what changed and deletes at the destination what is gone at the source. /MIR deletes, so check the destination twice.
/L lists what would be copied without copying anything: run it before the real copy.
Copies with owners, permissions and audit settings, in backup mode to pass files the account cannot read. Needs an elevated prompt.
Grants Modify to a group, inherited by subfolders (CI) and files (OI).
Saves the permissions of a whole tree; icacls D:\ /restore C:\Temp\acl.txt puts them back.
Takes ownership of a folder tree, answering yes for folders the account cannot list.
Deletes the .log files older than 30 days, subfolders included.
The state and process ID of a service.
Sets the start type: auto, demand or disabled. The space after start= is required.
The configuration of a service: binary path, start type, account and dependencies.
Every process with the services it hosts.
Ends every process with that name; /pid 1234 ends one process.
Every detail of a scheduled task, its last result included.
Creates a task running every night at 2:00 as SYSTEM.
Runs a task now.
Opens the disk partitioning prompt; the commands below are typed inside it.
In diskpart: the disks with their number, size and free space.
In diskpart: chooses the disk the next commands act on. Check the number against list disk.
In diskpart: erases the partition table of the selected disk. Everything on it is lost.
In diskpart: one partition using the whole disk.
In diskpart: formats the new partition.
In diskpart: gives the volume a drive letter.
Checks an NTFS volume online, without taking it offline; chkdsk D: /f repairs, and needs the volume unused.
The start-up entries and their settings.
Rebuilds the start-up files on the EFI system partition from the Windows installation, typically from WinRE.
Whether the Windows Recovery Environment is enabled, and where it lives.
BitLocker state of every volume: protection, encryption method and protectors.
The connections and listeners on port 443, with the process ID of each.

commands.command: netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="App 8443" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=8443
commands.description: Opens a TCP port inbound in the Windows Firewall.

commands.command: netsh wlan show profile name="Office" key=clear
commands.description: A saved Wi-Fi profile, its password included, from an elevated prompt.
The proxy Windows Update, BITS and the agents use, not the browser one.
The last 20 critical and error events of the System log.
Exports a whole log, to read on another machine or keep as evidence.
The SHA-256 of a file, to compare with the one the vendor publishes.
Builds the chain of a certificate and checks revocation (CRL and OCSP).
The certificates in the computer's personal store.
The account, its SID, groups and privileges in this session: elevated or not shows here.
Restarts now; shutdown /a cancels a shutdown that is counting down.

vendors.name: Intune and Entra device management
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. Join state, enrolment, synchronisation, Win32 apps and BitLocker keys on a Windows device managed with Microsoft Entra ID and Intune, read from the device itself.

commands.description: Join type (AzureAdJoined, DomainJoined, WorkplaceJoined), tenant, Primary Refresh Token, and the last registration error.
Asks for a new Primary Refresh Token for the signed-in user, after a password change or a Conditional Access fix.
Removes the Entra hybrid join or registration of the device. Run elevated, then restart; the device joins again at the next sync if still in scope.
The registration attempts and their errors.
MDM events: 75 is a successful automatic enrolment, 76 a failed one with its error.
The enrolment tasks, in one folder per enrolment ID.
Starts an Intune check-in now, as Sync does in Settings, Accounts, Access work or school.
Collects the MDM, Autopilot and TPM logs into one cab for support.
Writes MDMDiagReport.html: the policies and settings the device received and their state.
Follows the extension that installs Win32 apps and runs scripts and remediations.
The other logs: AppWorkload.log for app installs, AgentExecutor.log for scripts.
Makes the extension check again for assigned Win32 apps and scripts.
Install state of Win32 apps, per user and app ID.
At the out-of-box experience, opens a command prompt: the place to collect the hardware hash or read logs.
Exports the hardware hash to import the device into Autopilot.
The protectors of the system drive, with the recovery password ID to find the key in Entra ID or Intune.
Sends the recovery password with that ID to Microsoft Entra ID, for a key that was never escrowed.
Whether the TPM is present, ready and owned, as Autopilot and BitLocker need it.

vendors.name: Microsoft Graph and Exchange Online PowerShell
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. Users, licences, sessions and groups with the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK, and mailboxes, permissions and mail flow with the Exchange Online module. Both sign in interactively and act with the rights of the account used.

commands.description: Installs the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK for the current user.
Signs in and asks for the permissions named; an administrator may have to consent the first time.
The account, tenant and permissions of the current Graph session.
Installs the Exchange Online PowerShell module.
Signs in to Exchange Online; Disconnect-ExchangeOnline -Confirm:$false ends the session.

commands.command: Get-MgUser -UserId jane.doe@contoso.com -Property DisplayName, AccountEnabled, LastPasswordChangeDateTime | Format-List DisplayName, AccountEnabled, LastPasswordChangeDateTime
commands.description: The properties asked for: Graph returns only a few unless -Property names them.
Every disabled account.
The licences of a user.

commands.command: Get-MgSubscribedSku | Select-Object SkuPartNumber, ConsumedUnits, @{ Name = 'Available'; Expression = { $_.PrepaidUnits.Enabled } }
commands.description: Licences bought and used in the tenant.
Blocks sign-in for a user.
Invalidates the user's refresh tokens: every app must sign in again, within about an hour for access tokens already issued.
The MFA methods registered, to spot one an attacker added.
The latest sign-ins of a user with their result, application and location. Needs Entra ID P1.
A group by its name, with its ID.
The members of a group.
Adds a user to a group, by their IDs.

commands.command: Get-EXOMailboxStatistics -Identity jane.doe@contoso.com | Select-Object DisplayName, TotalItemSize, ItemCount
commands.description: Size and item count of a mailbox.
Full access to a shared mailbox, added to Outlook automatically.
Lets a user send as the shared mailbox.

commands.command: Get-InboxRule -Mailbox jane.doe@contoso.com | Select-Object Name, Enabled, MoveToFolder, DeleteMessage, ForwardTo
commands.description: Inbox rules: one hiding or forwarding mail from the bank or IT is a classic sign of a compromised mailbox.
Removes forwarding to an external address.

commands.command: Set-MailboxAutoReplyConfiguration -Identity jane.doe@contoso.com -AutoReplyState Enabled -InternalMessage 'Away until Monday.' -ExternalMessage 'Away until Monday.'
commands.description: Turns on the out of office message for someone who forgot.
What happened to messages sent to a user over two days: delivered, quarantined, failed. Older module versions use Get-MessageTrace.
Messages held in quarantine for a user.
Releases a quarantined message to its recipients.
DKIM signing state of each domain, and the selector records to publish.
The mail flow rules, in the order they apply.

vendors.name: OpenSSL and certificates
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. Reading, creating and converting certificates and keys with OpenSSL, as on Linux, macOS or Git for Windows, with the Windows equivalents. Private keys stay private: never paste one into a website.

commands.description: Who a certificate is for, who issued it, its validity dates and the names it covers.
Every field of a certificate, key usage and extensions included.
The SHA-256 fingerprint, as shown in browsers and Windows.
The content of a certificate request, and whether its signature is valid.
The chain a server really presents, and whether it verifies. -servername sends SNI, needed on shared hosting.
The certificate of a mail server after STARTTLS; imap, pop3 and ftp work the same way.
Whether a certificate chains up to the given CA certificates.
A private key and a certificate request with the names browsers check (subjectAltName).
A self-signed certificate for a lab.
An elliptic curve P-256 private key.
32 random bytes in Base64, for a secret or a key.

commands.description: Bundles a key, its certificate and the chain into a PFX that Windows imports.

Converts a DER (.cer) certificate to PEM.
Hash of the certificate's public key: compare it with the next command to know the key matches the certificate.
Hash of the public key derived from a private key.
Every field of a certificate file.

commands.description: Computer certificates expiring within 30 days.
A certificate request from an .inf file, with the key kept in the Windows store.
Exports a certificate with its private key, when the key was marked exportable.

vendors.name: tcpdump, Wireshark and Nmap
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. Capturing traffic on Linux and Windows, the Wireshark display filters that find a problem in a capture, and Nmap. Capture and scan only networks you are allowed to: a scan counts as an intrusion attempt in most security policies.

commands.description: Traffic between this machine and one host on one port, without name or port resolution.
Writes to rotating files of 100 MB, five at most, to open in Wireshark.
Only the connection attempts and resets of a saved capture.
Tagged frames with their link header, to see which VLAN reaches a trunk.
DHCP: discover, offer, request and acknowledge.
Captures whole packets with the built-in Packet Monitor, from an elevated prompt.
Stops the capture.
Converts the capture for Wireshark.

commands.command: netsh trace start capture=yes tracefile=C:\Temp\trace.etl maxsize=512

Everything to or from one address.
One TCP port, either direction.
Retransmissions: loss, or a path dropping large packets.
Resets: a refused connection or one torn down by a firewall.
DNS answers that are errors, such as NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL.
HTTP errors, in unencrypted traffic.
TLS connections to a site by the name the client asked for, without decrypting.
Kerberos errors, with the same codes as the domain controller events.
DHCP exchanges.
Everything from or to one MAC address.
Which hosts answer on a subnet, without scanning ports.
Whether these ports are open, and the service and version behind each.
Every TCP port of a host that does not answer ping.
UDP ports: DNS, NTP and SNMP. Needs administrator rights, and is slow.
The TLS versions and cipher suites a server accepts, graded.
Guesses the operating system from how the host answers.

vendors.name: Docker and Docker Compose
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. Running, reading and cleaning up containers, images, volumes and networks, and the Compose commands for a stack. The Docker Compose tool on the Tools page turns a docker run command into a Compose service.

commands.description: Every container, stopped ones included, with its status and ports.

The last 100 lines of a container's output, then follows it.
A shell inside a running container; bash where the image has it.

One field of the container's configuration or state.
Processor, memory and network use of each container, once.
Copies a file out of a container; swap the arguments to copy one in.
Local images with their tag and size.
Downloads an image; pin a tag rather than latest for anything that matters.
Builds an image from the Dockerfile in this folder.

commands.command: docker tag app:1.0 registry.contoso.com/app:1.0 && docker push registry.contoso.com/app:1.0
commands.description: Names an image for a registry and pushes it.
Removes every image no container uses.
Named volumes.

commands.description: Backs up a named volume into an archive in the current folder.
Networks: containers on the same user network reach each other by name.
A network shared by a reverse proxy and the containers behind it.
Creates and starts the stack of compose.yaml in the background.
The services of the stack and their state.
Follows the output of one service.

commands.command: docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
commands.description: Updates the images and recreates only the services that changed.

Space used by images, containers, volumes and build cache.

Engine version, storage driver, root folder and resources.

vendors.name: Kubernetes (kubectl)
vendors.description: Cheat sheet. Contexts, workloads, rollouts, services and the commands that explain why a pod does not run. -n names the namespace; the examples use web.
